title: Zoom Teaching How To Improve Learning, Attentiveness, And Self-Discipline ess-self-discipline/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin proposes a five-point 'preparation points' system to establish minimum success habits during Zoom lessons, adapting a strategy he already uses for in-person classroom management plans. Each student begins with five points and can lose them for logging in late, keeping video off, going off-screen, looking away from the screen too often, or leaving before the lesson ends. He argues these are not participation or behavior grades — which some districts prohibit — but baseline requirements tied directly to skills like preparation, collaboration, and listening that already appear in most curricula. He recommends the points count for a modest percentage of the overall grade, be introduced clearly during the first week of school, and be tracked passively (a mark on a roster) rather than announced in the moment, with responsibility for checking status placed on students and parents. He also directly rebuts the objection that mandatory video invades student privacy, arguing that allowing cameras off causes the rest of the class to disengage as well.
points: Award five 'preparation points' per Zoom lesson for logging in on time, camera on, staying on-screen, watching the screen, and staying to the end.
Frame these as minimum success requirements tied to existing curriculum language, not as participation or behavior grades.
Deduct points quietly with a mark on a roster rather than announcing losses to the student in the moment.
Update grades online at least weekly so students and parents can check status on their own time.
Allowing cameras to be optional causes most of the class to follow suit and disengage, undermining the whole lesson.
quotes: In fact, success preparedness has been so de-emphasized in recent years that teaching it has become a lost art.
As you can see, they’re very basic—representing the least that is required for success in a Zoom or Google Meet lesson. But they’re also crucial.
The point system represents the essential bones for each of these skills. They must be in place first if you hope to make video distance learning effective.
It’s important to mention that preparation points are not a reward. They’re an evaluation. As such, an easy way to manage them is to have every student start off with 5 points.

First of all, if you allow them to turn their video function off, then all hope is lost. Most of your class will follow suit, and even if they are in front of their screens—which is highly questionable—very little learning is going to take place.
